faqs.a: Yes, and nobody will mind — নমস্কার is understood everywhere in Bengal. But friends will smile, because it sounds formal. With friends try কী খবর? (ki khobor — what's new?) instead.
faqs.q: Can I just say namaskar?

faqs.a: নমস্কার with folded hands and a small nod, and use আপনি (apni — formal you) until they invite you to তুমি. Add দাদা (dada) or দিদি (didi) for someone a little older — it warms everything.
faqs.q: How do I greet an elder respectfully?

faqs.a: You ask leave instead of saying goodbye: আসি (ashi — I'm off). The other person answers এসো (esho — come again). It is one of the loveliest small customs in the language.
faqs.q: How do Bengalis say goodbye?

topics.lede: নমস্কার opens every door in Bengal — but friends, elders and goodbyes each have their own rules.
paras: নমস্কার (nomoshkar) is the one greeting that never fails. Folded hands, a small nod, and it works with strangers, elders, shopkeepers and officials — exactly the people a learner meets first. Muslim Bengalis often greet with আসসালামু আলাইকুম or the shorter আদাব (adab); if someone greets you that way, answering the same way is both correct and courteous.

Friends do not nomoshkar each other — it would sound like a speech. They ask কী খবর? (ki khobor — what's the news?) or simply start talking. A useful halfway step is দাদা (dada — elder brother) or দিদি (didi — elder sister) for anyone a little older than you, relative or not. A rickshaw puller called দাদা will quite literally take better care of you.

Bengali has three levels of you, and this is the part worth learning early. আপনি (apni) is formal — strangers, elders, anyone you respect. তুমি (tumi) is for friends, peers and younger family. তুই (tui) is intimate — small children, your closest friends, and God. When unsure, আপনি is never wrong; sliding down to তুমি happens naturally when someone invites it.

And goodbye: Bengalis rarely say anything as final as goodbye. The person leaving says আসি (ashi — I'm off, I'll be back), and the person staying answers এসো (esho — do come again). For thanks, ধন্যবাদ (dhonnobad) works everywhere; অনেক ধন্যবাদ (many thanks) costs nothing extra and buys real warmth.

faqs.a: Cousins, not twins. Both hang words from a headline and both descend from the same ancient script, but the letter shapes differ and Bengali pronounces its built-in vowel as aw where Hindi says a. One does not read the other.
faqs.q: Is the Bengali script the same as Hindi's?

faqs.a: A focused learner reads slowly within two weeks and comfortably within two months. Writing your own name on day one is the traditional — and correct — way to start.
faqs.q: How long does the alphabet take?

faqs.a: No. Conjuncts are just two letters sharing one body — ক্ষ is ক plus ষ. Learn them inside real words (which this course does) and they stop looking scary within days.

topics.h1: The Bengali alphabet: less scary than it looks
topics.lede: Fifty letters, one honest script — and the single sound that separates learners from real speakers.
paras: The Bengali script has eleven vowels (স্বরবর্ণ) and thirty-nine consonants (ব্যঞ্জনবর্ণ). It runs left to right, and like its cousin Devanagari it hangs words from a horizontal headline. Every consonant carries a built-in vowel — ক is not just k, it is kaw. That built-in vowel is the whole game, so let us say it plainly.

In Bengali the built-in vowel অ sounds like the o in English hot — an aw sound — not the flat a of Hindi. So কলকাতা is Kawlkata, never Kalkata. Learners coming from Hindi get this wrong for months; learners who fix it on day one sound strikingly better for almost no effort. This single habit is the cheapest upgrade in the language.

A few letters deserve a personal introduction. য় sounds like y in yes. ড় and ঢ় are flaps — put your tongue where it goes for the tt in American butter and you are nearly there. ং, ঃ and ঁ are nasal marks that colour the vowel beside them rather than sounding on their own. And ৎ (khanda-ta) is a t with its vowel chopped off, ending words like হঠাৎ (hothat — suddenly).

Then there are the joint letters, যুক্তাক্ষর — two or three consonants sharing one body, like ক্ষ or জ্ঞ. They look frightening in a chart and feel ordinary in real words, because only a handful are common. Do not memorise the chart; meet each conjunct inside a word you actually want, the way children do.
Start here: the eleven vowels, then the first row ক খ গ ঘ ঙ, then your own name. Write a little every day — the script was designed by hand and it only surrenders to the hand.

topics.note: A note on romanisation. There is no single official way to write Bengali in Latin letters — you will see aw, o and ô for অ, and ch, cch and chh for ছ. This course picks the spelling closest to the actual sound and sticks to it. Learn the script itself and the problem disappears.

topics.desc: এক দুই তিন to একশো — plus the little counting words টা and জন that textbooks always forget. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Both, mixed freely. Shop signs, bus numbers and clocks usually show Bengali digits; phone numbers and prices are often in international digits. Learn to read Bengali digits first — that is the direction you cannot fake.
faqs.q: Which digits will I actually see in Bengal?

faqs.a: Little counting words that sit between the number and the noun: একটা বই (one book), দুজন মানুষ (two people). Skip them and you sound like a textbook; use them and you sound like a person.
faqs.q: What are counters (টা, জন)?

faqs.a: দাম কত? (dam koto — how much?). Then listen for the number plus টাকা (taka). Market Bengali is the fastest teacher there is.
faqs.q: How do I ask the price of something?

topics.lede: এক দুই তিন — plus the little counting words that textbooks forget and markets demand.
paras: Bengali digits — ০১২৩৪৫৬৭৮৯ — are everywhere in Bengal: price tags, bus numbers, clocks, exam papers. International digits appear too, but the Bengali set is the one you cannot fake, so learn to read it first. The shapes are friendly: ১ ২ ৩ are barely disguised cousins of 1 2 3.

The words one to ten are এক, দুই, তিন, চার, পাঁচ, ছয়, সাত, আট, নয়, দশ. Eleven to twenty go their own way (এগারো, বারো, তেরো…), and then the tens take over: বিশ (20), তিরিশ (30), চল্লিশ (40), পঞ্চাশ (50), ষাট (60), সত্তর (70), আশি (80), নব্বই (90), একশো (100). Past twenty, numbers are built by glueing tens to units — একুশ (21), বত্রিশ (32) — and hearing them in a market teaches them faster than any list.

Now the part textbooks skip: you almost never put a bare number next to a noun. Things take টা — একটা বই (one book), তিনটে আম (three mangoes). People take জন — একজন মানুষ (one person), দুজন বন্ধু (two friends). Using the bare number is understood and instantly marks you as foreign; the counters are small words with an outsized payoff.

Two places to spend your new numbers immediately. Money: the currency is the টাকা (taka), and দাম কত? (dam koto — how much?) is the most useful sentence in Bengal. Time: the clock reuses টা in a special form — তিনটে means three o'clock. Learn that one sentence and that one clock trick, and your numbers are already earning their keep.
topics.title: Bengali numbers 1–100
topics.note: A note on টা becoming টে. Counters shift shape in real speech: একটা (one thing) but তিনটে (three o'clock), দুটো (two things). Natives never think about it and learners should not memorise tables of it — hear each form inside its sentence, on this page and in the market lessons, and the pattern absorbs itself.

faqs.a: আপনার নাম কী? (apnar nam ki). Answer with আমার নাম … (amar nam …). Then ask back: আর আপনার? It is the friendliest three seconds in the language.
faqs.q: How do I ask someone's name?

faqs.a: বুঝতে পারছি না (bujhte parchi na — I don't understand), আস্তে বলুন (aste bolun — please speak slowly) and আবার বলুন (abar bolun — please say it again). These three sentences rescue every conversation.
faqs.q: What do I say when I don't understand?

faqs.a: Yes — ঠিক আছে (thik achhe) is the universal softener: okay, agreed, got it, fine. Nod while saying it and half of daily life runs itself.
faqs.q: Is there one all-purpose word?

topics.note: A note on code-switching. Real Bengali conversation mixes in English constantly — time, market, bill, okay. This is not broken Bengali; it is how the language is actually spoken in cities. Use the English word without shame when the Bengali one escapes you.
paras: Every Bengali conversation you will ever have starts the same way: a name, a place, a little warmth. আপনার নাম কী? (apnar nam ki — what is your name?), আমি … থেকে এসেছি (ami … theke esechi — I have come from …). Ask where someone is from before you ask what they do — roots interest Bengalis more than jobs, and the question always lands well.

The market is your second classroom. কটা? or দাম কত? (how much?), দামটা একটু কমান (damta ektu koman — lower the price a little), ঠিক আছে, নিলাম (thik achhe, nilam — okay, I'll take it). Bargain with a smile and accept the final price gracefully; the performance is the point, and both sides know it.

Small talk runs on three rails: food (খেয়েছেন? — have you eaten?), family, and the weather during monsoon. কী খবর? (ki khobor — what's new?) is not really a question — answer with ভালো, আপনি বলুন (bhalo, apni bolun — good, you tell me) and the conversation rolls.

And when you get lost — you will, daily — three rescue lines save you: বুঝতে পারছি না (I don't understand), আস্তে বলুন (speak slowly, please), আবার বলুন (say it again, please). Said with a smile, they make Bengalis slow down and lean in. Getting lost is not failure; it is the lesson.

topics.desc: করি, করলে, করব — present, past, future with zero jargon, plus the হই/আছি split. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Both mean am/is, split by meaning: হই (hoi) for identity — আমি ছাত্র (I am a student) — and আছি (achhi) for state and place — আমি ভালো আছি (I am fine), আমি বাড়িতে আছি (I am at home). Mix them and you still get understood; split them and you sound right.
faqs.q: What is the difference between হই and আছি?

faqs.a: Endings, not separate words. আমি করি (I do), তুমি করো (you do), আপনি করেন (you do, formal). Learn the three endings for one verb and you can conjugate nearly every verb you meet.
faqs.q: How do I say I/you do something?

faqs.a: Lengthen the past: করলাম (I did), করলে (you did), করলেন (you did, formal). One extra ল sound carries the whole past tense.
faqs.q: How do I talk about yesterday?

topics.note: A note on করব vs করবো. You will see the future ending written both ways — করব and করবো. Both are the same word; the extra ো marks the o sound explicitly. Spelling wobbles like this are normal in Bengali; pronounce the o either way.
paras: Bengali verbs are kinder than they look. Take করা (kora — to do): the root কর never changes, and small endings do all the work. Present tense: আমি করি (ami kori — I do), তুমি করো (tumi koro — you do), আপনি করেন (apni koren — you do, formal). Three endings, and the pattern repeats across almost every verb in the language.

The past adds one sound: ল. করলাম (korlam — I did), করলে (korle — you did), করলেন (korlen — you did, formal). The future adds ব: করব (korbo — I will do), করবে (korbe — you will), করবেন (korben — you will, formal). Present, past, future — three endings each, all built on the same root.

The verb to be splits in two, and this split is the most useful thing on this page. হই (hoi) is for identity: আমি ছাত্র (ami chhatro — I am a student). আছি (achhi) is for state and place: আমি ভালো আছি (I am fine), আমি বাড়িতে আছি (I am at home). Identity versus situation — feel that difference and half of Bengali sentences unlock.

Start with five verbs and refuse to add a sixth until these are automatic: করা (do), যাওয়া (go), আসা (come), খাওয়া (eat), দেওয়া (give). Everything you want to say in your first month is built from these five plus nouns. Fluency is not knowing many verbs; it is these five at speed.

faqs.a: Both mean water, split by community: Hindu families tend to say জল (jol), Muslim families পানি (pani). Everyone understands both. Use whichever you hear around you — matching your surroundings is the whole trick.
faqs.q: জল or পানি — which word for water?

faqs.a: দাদা (dada — elder brother) and দিদি (didi — elder sister) stretch far beyond blood: use them for any slightly-older man or woman and doors open. It is respect disguised as family.
faqs.q: Why does everyone call strangers দাদা?

faqs.a: Ten a day, out loud, in sentences — never bare lists. বড় বাড়ি (big house) sticks; বড় alone evaporates. Attach every new word to something you can see.

topics.note: A note on Hindu and Muslim words. Bengali has gentle doublets from its two communities — জল/পানি (water), নিমন্ত্রণ/দাওয়াত (invitation). Neither is wrong and everyone understands both. Learn your surroundings' version first, recognise the other.
paras: A hundred words carry most of daily life, and this page holds the first third of them. Start with people: বাবা (baba — father), মা (ma — mother), ভাই (bhai — brother), বোন (bon — sister), ছেলে (chhele — boy/son), মেয়ে (meye — girl/daughter). Then stretch দাদা and দিদি to every slightly-older stranger — family words are also respect words.

Colours come next because the market demands them: লাল (lal — red), নীল (neel — blue), সবুজ (shobuj — green), হলুদ (holud — yellow), সাদা (shada — white), কালো (kalo — black). Point and ask এটা কী রঙ? (eta ki rong — what colour is this?) and shopkeepers become teachers.

Then the adjectives that judge everything: ভালো (bhalo — good), খারাপ (kharap — bad), বড় (boro — big), ছোট (chhoto — small), নতুন (notun — new), পুরনো (purono — old). And the nouns of home: বাড়ি (bari — house), জল (jol — water), ভাত (bhat — rice), বই (boi — book). Twenty words, and you can already want things out loud.

Learn ten words a day, always out loud, always inside a sentence. বড় বাড়ি (big house) sticks in memory; বড় floating alone evaporates by evening. Attach each word to something you can see, touch or eat — vocabulary learned through the senses stays for years.

topics.desc: ঝাল কম, আরেকটা দিন, বিল দিন — eat well from day one, veg or not. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: ঝাল কম দিন (jhal kom din — make it less spicy). Say it with a smile when ordering and every kitchen understands. Bengali heat is flavourful rather than fierce, but restaurant spice assumes local stomachs.
faqs.q: How do I ask for less spicy food?

faqs.a: আমি নিরামিষ খাই (ami niramish khai — I eat vegetarian). Bengal loves its fish and meat, but pure-veg cooking is deep and respected — ডাল, শাক, সবজি done properly need no apology.
faqs.q: I am vegetarian — what do I say?

faqs.a: বিল দিন (bill din — give the bill). In small eateries the bill comes on memory and a scrap of paper; check it with good humour, pay, and say খুব ভালো ছিল (it was very good).
faqs.q: How do I ask for the bill?

topics.note: A note on মাছ. মাছ (machh — fish) is not a side dish in Bengal; it is the centre of the cuisine and, many would say, of civilisation. Even the phrase মাছে-ভাতে বাঙালি (fish-and-rice Bengali) defines the people. Respect the fish and Bengal respects you.
paras: Bengali food runs on rice and rhythm: ভাত (bhat — rice), ডাল (dal — lentils), ভাজা (bhaja — fried), মাছ (machh — fish), মাংস (mangsho — meat), চাটনি (chatni — chutney), মিষ্টি (mishti — sweets). Order by pointing and naming: ভাত-ডাল দিন (bhat-dal din — give rice-lentils). Meals arrive in waves; pace yourself.

Season your order like a local. ঝাল কম (jhal kom — less spicy), মিষ্টি কম (mishti kom — less sweet, for tea and desserts), গরম গরম (gorom gorom — piping hot, the highest praise for fried food). These three adjustments mark you as someone who eats with attention, and kitchens respond to attention.

Praise is a social duty. খুব মজা (khub moja — very tasty), দারুণ হয়েছে (darun hoyechhe — it's turned out superb), আরেকটা দিন (arekta din — give one more). The cook — professional or grandmother — runs on this fuel. Eat everything offered seconds of; refusal needs the shield of পেট ভরে গেছে (pet bhore gechhe — my stomach is full).

End with ceremony: বিল দিন (bill din — the bill, please), pay with a smile, and finish with খুব ভালো ছিল (khub bhalo chhilo — it was very good). Then walk — ভাতঘুম (bhatghum — the rice-sleep) is real, and the evening adda (chat session) over চা is where the day's Bengali gets reviewed.

topics.desc: The aw-sound, the three sh-letters, ড় vs র — sound Bengali, not textbook. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Like aw in English law: ক is kaw, কথা is kotha. At the end of words অ often rounds fully to o. This one sound is the audible line between Hindi speakers trying Bengali and real Bengali speakers.
faqs.q: How is অ really pronounced?

faqs.a: To a learner's ear, yes — all three (শ ষ স) sound like English sh in most Kolkata speech. Say sh for all of them and refine later; nobody will misunderstand you.
faqs.q: Are শ, ষ and স all the same sound?

faqs.a: র is a light trill/tap, ড় is the English-like flap (like the tt in American butter). Wrong one, wrong word: করা (kora — to do) versus কড়া (kora — strict). Minimal pairs are the gym for this distinction.
faqs.q: র vs ড় — what is the difference?

topics.note: A note on the final -o. Word-final অ rounds to o: কথা is kotha not kawtha, ভালো is bhalo. Middle অ stays aw: কলকাতা is Kawlkata. Final-o, middle-aw — chant it until it is reflex.
paras: Six sounds carry Bengali pronunciation, and the first is the famous one: অ is aw, as in English law. ক is kaw, গান is gaan… wait, no — গান keeps its া (aa), which is exactly the point: only the built-in অ says aw. And at word ends it rounds further to o: কথা (kotha), ভালো (bhalo).

Second: the three sh-letters. শ, ষ and স all sound like English sh in modern Kolkata speech — শহর (shohor), কষ্ট (koshto), সকাল (shokal). Purists keep subtle distinctions; learners should say sh everywhere and be understood everywhere. One less thing to fear.

Third and fourth: the r-family. র is a light tap or trill (রাত — rat, night). ড় is the flap — tongue flicks like the tt in American butter (বড় — boro, big). Mix them and words change meaning, so drill minimal pairs: করা/কড়া, পড়া/পরা. Fifth: য় is just y (মেয়ে — meye). Sixth: ছ is breathy chh — push air through ছেলে (chhele, boy).

Two traps to dodge. Trap one: stress sits early and light — Bengali does not punch syllables like English. Trap two: the ো vs অ ending (bhalo not bhalaw). Record yourself reading this page's table, compare with the speaker buttons at 0.2×, and fix one sound a week. In six weeks you will sound like someone's neighbour.

topics.desc: SOV order, postpositions, no gender, কী vs কি — grammar without tears. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Subject-Object-Verb: আমি ভাত খাই (I rice eat). The verb always comes last — train yourself to hold the verb until the end and Bengali word order clicks within days.
faqs.q: What is Bengali word order?

faqs.a: কী (ki — with long ী) asks what: এটা কী? (what is this?). কি (ki — short ি) asks yes/no: তুমি যাবে কি? (will you go?). Same sound, different spelling, different job — written Bengali cares, spoken Bengali doesn't.
faqs.q: কী vs কি — what is the difference?

faqs.a: There is none — adjectives and verbs never change for gender. বড় ছেলে, বড় মেয়ে: same বড়. After Hindi or French, this feels like a holiday.
faqs.q: Does Bengali have grammatical gender?

topics.note: A note on না vs নি. Present negation uses না after the verb (খাই না — don't eat); past negation fuses into নি (খাইনি — didn't eat). Two shapes, one habit: negate late, at the verb, where Bengali puts everything important.
paras: Bengali sentences end with the verb — always. আমি ভাত খাই (ami bhat khai — I rice eat). ইংরেজি শিখছি (English am-learning). Whatever the sentence carries, the verb waits at the gate. English speakers must learn to hold their verb back; once that reflex forms, Bengali order feels inevitable rather than backwards.

English has prepositions (before nouns); Bengali has postpositions (after them). বাড়িতে (barite — in the house), টেবিলের উপর (on the table), আমার জন্য (for me), তোমার সাথে (with you). The helper-word leans on its noun from behind — same logic as the verb waiting at the end. Bengali is a language that finishes its thoughts late.

Then the great gift: no grammatical gender. Adjectives never change — বড় ছেলে, বড় মেয়ে, বড় বাড়ি: same বড় everywhere. Verbs care about person (I/you/he) but never about masculine or feminine. Every hour Hindi or French learners spend on gender, you spend on words.

Questions and negatives are small. What-questions use কী (এটা কী? — what is this?); yes/no questions use কি (যাবে কি? — will you go?). Negation sits at the verb: খাই না (don't eat), খাইনি (didn't eat), খাবো না (won't eat). Verb last, helpers behind, negate late — that is ninety percent of Bengali grammar.

faqs.a: No. Start with spoken Bengali in Roman letters, and let the script come second. Learners who speak first and read later stay motivated far longer than learners who drill the alphabet for a month before saying a word.
faqs.q: Must I learn the Bengali script before speaking?

faqs.a: Ten focused minutes beats an hour of passive app-tapping. Say every new word out loud three times, then use it in one real sentence about your own life. The mouth learns what the eyes only visit.
faqs.q: How much should I study every day?

faqs.a: নমস্কার for respect, হ্যাঁ and না, ধন্যবাদ, দয়া করে, ঠিক আছে, and আমি — I. With those seven you can open any interaction in Bengal politely while your vocabulary grows underneath.

topics.note: A note on the Roman letters. The Sounds like column is training wheels, not the bicycle. Sh covers three Bengali letters (শ ষ স) that all sound like sh in real speech, and o at a word's end is often silent — ধন্যবাদ sounds like dhonnobad, not dhonnobada. Use the Roman to start speaking today; let the script fix your pronunciation tomorrow.
paras: Every Bengali journey starts with the same seven keys: নমস্কার (nomoshkar — hello), হ্যাঁ (hyã — yes), না (na — no), ধন্যবাদ (dhonnobad — thank you), দয়া করে (doya kore — please), ঠিক আছে (thik achhe — okay), and আমি (ami — I). Memorise nothing else in week one. These seven open doors, buy patience, and give every stranger a reason to help you with word number eight.

Your first sentence needs only three of them: আমি ঠিক আছি (ami thik achhi — I am fine). Say it out loud right now, three times, and you have crossed the hardest border in language learning — the one between studying Bengali and speaking it. Everything after this is just more words in the same brave mouth.

Forget the alphabet for the first week. Spoken Bengali first, script second — that order keeps learners going, while script-first learners usually quit somewhere around the eleventh vowel sign. When you are ready, the alphabet page teaches the letters through words you already speak, so nothing you learn now is ever wasted.

The ten-minute plan: minutes one to three, say yesterday's words aloud. Minutes four to seven, learn three new words and use each in one sentence about your own life — আমার চা ভালো লাগে (I like tea) beats any flashcard. Minutes eight to ten, listen to one dialogue and shadow it, mumbling along half a beat behind. Ten minutes, every day, out loud: that is the whole method.

topics.desc: মা, বাবা, দাদা, দিদি — and the uncles and aunties that make Bengal feel like one big family. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Yes — দাদা (older brother) and দিদি (older sister) are the default respectful address for anyone slightly older, related or not. Shopkeepers, auto drivers, colleagues: দাদা and দিদি warm every interaction in Bengal.
faqs.q: Can I call strangers দাদা and দিদি?

faqs.a: A কাকা is your father's brother; a মামা is your mother's brother. Bengali keeps the two sides of the family strictly separate, and mixing them up is the classic learner slip — when in doubt, ask কার ভাই? (whose brother?) and smile.
faqs.q: What is the difference between কাকা and মামা?

faqs.a: Both exist, with দাদু leaning paternal and নানা leaning maternal in many families — but usage varies by family, so copy whatever the grandchildren say. Nobody grades you on grandparents.
faqs.q: দাদু or নানা for grandfather?

topics.note: A note on বউদি and জামাইবাবু. Bengali has exact words for in-laws that English collapses into one vague in-law — your elder brother's wife is বউদি (boudi), your sister's husband জামাইবাবু (jamai-babu). You do not need these in month one, but when a Bengali family adopts you — and one will — they will teach you your exact title with great ceremony.
paras: Start at the centre: মা (ma — mother), বাবা (baba — father), দাদা (dada — elder brother), দিদি (didi — elder sister), ভাই (bhai — younger brother), বোন (bon — younger sister). Bengali sorts siblings by age, not just gender — দাদা versus ভাই is about who is older, and getting it right signals that you see the family the way it sees itself.

Then come the sides. Father's side: কাকা (kaka — uncle) and কাকিমা (kakima — aunt). Mother's side: মামা (mama — uncle) and মামি (mami — aunt). Father's sister is পিসি (pishi); mother's sister is মাসি (mashi). Four different aunties and uncles where English has two — learn them as pairs and they stick fast.

Here is the secret that makes family words the most useful vocabulary in Bengali: দাদা and দিদি escape the family entirely. The tea-stall owner is দাদা, the colleague is দিদি, the helpful stranger becomes কাকা within minutes. Bengali turns transactions into relationships by promoting everyone to family — join in, and prices soften and smiles widen.

Grandparents complete the picture: দাদু (dadu) and ঠাকুমা (thakuma) on one side, নানা (nana) and দিদিমা (didima) on the other, with exact sides varying by family. And children: ছেলে (chhele — boy/son) and মেয়ে (meye — girl/daughter), plus বাচ্চা (bachcha — small child) for the little ones who will correct your pronunciation without mercy.

topics.desc: আজ, কাল, পরশু — days, clock time, and the famous কাল that means yesterday AND tomorrow. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Yes — কাল means yesterday looking back and tomorrow looking forward; tense and context choose. Learners panic, natives never notice: গতকাল (gotokal — yesterday) and আগামীকাল (agamikal — tomorrow) exist for the rare moments when it truly matters.
faqs.q: Does কাল really mean both yesterday and tomorrow?

faqs.a: Take the number, add টা: তিনটে (three o'clock), পাঁচটা (five o'clock). Half past adds সাড়ে (sare) — সাড়ে তিনটে is half past three. Bengali clock time is one small rule with an enormous payoff.
faqs.q: How do I say the time in Bengali?

faqs.a: রবিবার (Sunday) first, then সোমবার through শনিবার. Six of the seven end in -বার (bar — day), so learn রবি, সোম, মঙ্গল, বুধ, বৃহস্পতি, শুক্র, শনি and the week assembles itself.
faqs.q: What order do the Bengali weekdays go in?

topics.note: A note on সাড়ে, সোয়া and পৌনে. Bengali slices the hour three ways: সোয়া (shoa — quarter past), সাড়ে (sare — half past), পৌনে (poune — quarter to). সোয়া চারটে is quarter past four; পৌনে পাঁচটা is quarter to five. Three little words, and you can read every clock and catch every train in Bengal.
paras: Anchor yourself with five words: আজ (aaj — today), কাল (kal — yesterday/tomorrow), পরশু (porshu — day after tomorrow), এখন (ekhon — now), পরে (pore — later). Five words cover ninety percent of daily planning — কাল আসুন (come tomorrow) and পরে কথা হবে (we'll talk later) will carry you through weeks of real life.

The week runs রবিবার (robibar — Sunday), সোমবার (shombar — Monday), মঙ্গলবার (mongolbar — Tuesday), বুধবার (budhbar — Wednesday), বৃহস্পতিবার (brihoshpotibar — Thursday), শুক্রবার (shukrobar — Friday), শনিবার (shonibar — Saturday). Thursday's name is the week's heavyweight — practise brihoshpotibar slowly and the rest of the week feels easy.

Clock time is beautifully simple: number plus টা. একটা (one o'clock), দুটো (two o'clock — note the change!), তিনটে (three o'clock), চারটে, পাঁচটা. এখন কটা বাজে? (ekhon kota baje — what time is it now?) is the question; the answer is just the number with its টা. Two and three bend the rule (দুটো, তিনটে) — learn those two exceptions and the clock is yours.

Parts of the day paint every plan: সকাল (shokal — morning), দুপুর (dupur — midday), বিকেল (bikel — afternoon), সন্ধ্যা (shondha — evening), রাত (raat — night). সকালে (in the morning) and রাতে (at night) add one small -এ sound — সকালে যাব (I'll go in the morning) — and suddenly your sentences have schedules.

topics.desc: ডান, বাম, সোজা — directions, fares, tickets and the sentences that get you there. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Start with the place, end with যাব (jabo — will go): স্টেশন যাব (station jabo — I'll go to the station). Add ভাড়া কত? (bhara koto — how much is the fare?) before you sit down, and you will travel Bengal at local prices.
faqs.q: How do I tell a taxi driver where to go?

faqs.a: এটা কোথায়? (eta kothay — where is this?) while pointing at the address on your phone. Pointing plus three words beats a paragraph of memorised grammar every single time.
faqs.q: How do I ask where something is?

faqs.a: থামুন (thamun — please stop). Say it early, say it clearly, and have the fare ready — Bengal's drivers stop fast and appreciate passengers who do the same.
faqs.q: How do I ask the driver to stop?

topics.note: A note on যাব, খাব, করব. The future tense in Bengali is almost suspiciously easy: verb stem plus -ব (bo). যাব (jabo — will go), খাব (khabo — will eat), দেখব (dekhbo — will see). One ending, every verb, no exceptions that matter — the future is the first tense that makes learners grin.
paras: Directions are three words plus pointing: ডান (dan — right), বাম (bam — left), সোজা (shoja — straight). ডানদিকে যান (go to the right side), বামদিকে (to the left), সোজা যান (go straight). Add সামনে (shamne — ahead) and পেছনে (pechhone — behind), and you can follow any set of directions a helpful stranger draws in the air.

Every journey starts with two questions. কত দূর? (koto dur — how far?) tells you whether to walk or ride. ভাড়া কত? (bhara koto — how much is the fare?) asked BEFORE sitting down is the difference between the local price and the tourist price. Memorise these two before you memorise anything else on this page.

Stations and stops have their own vocabulary: বাস স্টপ (bus stop), রেল স্টেশন (rail station), টিকিট কাউন্টার (ticket counter), প্ল্যাটফর্ম (platform). টিকিট (ticket) plus your destination plus দিন (din — give) buys almost anything: একটা টিকিট দিন (one ticket please). Platforms are announced in Bengali first — শিয়ালদহ প্ল্যাটফর্মে (on Sealdah platform) is the kind of sentence your ears will learn to catch.

In the vehicle, three sentences cover everything: চলুন (cholun — let's go), থামুন (thamun — please stop), এখানে (ekhane — here). পৌঁছে গেছি (pouche gechhi — I've arrived) closes the journey with a smile. Drivers in Bengal respect passengers who speak even ten words — speak them, and the city starts helping you.

topics.desc: দাম কত? কম হবে? — prices, bargaining and market Bengali that pays for itself. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: In markets and small shops, always — start around two-thirds of the asking price and meet in the middle with a smile. In malls and fixed-price shops, never; the price tag is the price. কম হবে? (kom hobe — will it come down?) asked cheerfully is the whole technique.
faqs.q: Should I bargain in Bengal?

faqs.a: দুটো and তিনটে, never bare দুই and তিন before a noun. Things take টা/টে (একটা শাড়ি — one sari), people take জন. Counters are the fastest way to sound like a buyer instead of a tourist.
faqs.q: How do I count things I am buying?

faqs.a: শুধু দেখছি (shudhu dekhchhi — just looking), with a smile. It is respected everywhere and frees you to browse ten shops before buying in the eleventh.
faqs.q: How do I say I am just looking?

topics.note: A note on দাম, মূল্য and ভাড়া. দাম (dam) is the price of things, ভাড়া (bhara) is the fare for rides and rent — never swap them. মূল্য (mullo) is the formal written word for price, seen on bills and boards. Three words, three worlds: দাম কত? in the shop, ভাড়া কত? in the taxi, মূল্য on the receipt.
paras: The market runs on one question: দাম কত? (dam koto — how much?). The answer comes as a number plus টাকা (taka) — পঞ্চাশ টাকা (fifty taka). Listen for the number, repeat it back to confirm — পঞ্চাশ? — and you have completed your first Bengali transaction before you know any grammar at all.

Then comes the dance. বেশি দাম (beshi dam — too expensive), said thoughtfully, opens bargaining anywhere outside fixed-price shops. কম হবে? (kom hobe — will it come down?) is the direct question; ছাড় দিন (chhar din — give a discount) is its bolder cousin. Start near two-thirds, meet in the middle, smile throughout — bargaining in Bengal is a friendly game, and grim faces lose.

Count what you buy like a local: একটা (one thing), দুটো (two things), তিনটে (three things). এক কেজি আলু (one kilo of potatoes), দুটো শাড়ি দেখি (let me see two saris — দেখি, dekhi, is the magic browsing word). Shopkeepers hear the counters and switch you from tourist prices to real prices.

Close the deal with three sentences: এটা নেব (eta nebo — I'll take this), ঠিক আছে (thik achhe — agreed), ধন্যবাদ (dhonnobad — thank you). And the escape hatch every browser needs: শুধু দেখছি (shudhu dekhchhi — just looking), which is honoured in every market in Bengal without a flicker of annoyance.

faqs.a: সাহায্য করুন! (shahajjo korun — please help!), loud and clear, then point at the problem. In a real emergency nobody grades your grammar — volume, pointing and the word ডাক্তার (doctor) communicate everything.
faqs.q: What is the single most important emergency word?

faqs.a: জল (jol) in West Bengal, পানি (pani) in Bangladesh — same water, different word, and a famous shibboleth between the two Bengals. জল দিন (jol din — give water) works everywhere on the Indian side.
faqs.q: জল or পানি for water?

faqs.a: আমার ওষুধ লাগবে (amar oshudh lagbe — I need my medicine) and keep the prescription on your phone. Pharmacy staff in Bengal cities usually read English prescriptions without trouble.
faqs.q: How do I explain I need medicine?

topics.note: A note on করুন, দিন, ডাকুন. Emergency Bengali runs on three polite commands: করুন (korun — please do), দিন (din — please give), ডাকুন (dakun — please call). ডাক্তার ডাকুন (call a doctor), জল দিন (give water), সাহায্য করুন (please help). Three verbs, infinite emergencies — and the politeness costs nothing even when seconds count.
paras: Learn this page backwards: start with সাহায্য করুন! (shahajjo korun — please help!), ডাক্তার (daktar — doctor), হাসপাতাল (hashpatal — hospital), পুলিশ (pulish — police). Four words, and any crowd in Bengal will organise itself around you — Bengalis help first and ask questions later, especially when a foreigner speaks their language in trouble.

The body has its own vocabulary: ব্যথা (byatha — pain), জ্বর (jwor — fever), ওষুধ (oshudh — medicine), রক্ত (rokto — blood). এখানে ব্যথা (pain here), pointing, is a complete medical consultation for starters. আমার ডাক্তার লাগবে (I need a doctor) is never misunderstood and never ignored.

Being lost is the friendliest emergency: আমি হারিয়ে গেছি (ami hariye gechhi — I am lost) turns every stranger into a guide. Add your hotel's name plus কোথায়? and follow the pointing armada — in Bengal, lost foreigners get escorted, not just directed. Keep your hotel card in your pocket and your phone charged.

Two practical sentences close the kit: ফোন করতে পারি? (phone korte pari — may I make a call?) and ঠিকানা লিখে দিন (thikana likhe din — please write the address). Paper, pen, pointing and politeness solve what vocabulary cannot — and দয়া করে (please) said with eye contact has rescued more travellers than any phrasebook.

topics.desc: আপনি, তুমি, তুই — three yous, three verb endings, and the social map of Bengal. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Start with আপনি for every adult you don't know well — it is never wrong, only occasionally too formal, and Bengalis simply smile and invite you down to তুমি. Starting too casual is the only real mistake.
faqs.q: Which you should a beginner use?

faqs.a: For close friends, children, and affection — তুই with a stranger is an insult, তুই with your best friend is love. Learners should understand it, rarely say it, and let friends invite them into it.
faqs.q: When is তুই okay?

faqs.a: It's the old literary style (সাধু ভাষা) versus today's living language (চলিত ভাষা) — তাহারা versus তারা for they. Read the old style in Tagore; speak the new style everywhere. This page teaches the living one.

topics.note: A note on করি, করো, করেন. Every verb wears its politeness on its ending: আমি করি (I do), তুমি করো (you do, familiar), আপনি করেন (you do, formal). Learn one verb in all three forms — করা (to do) is the classic — and the whole politeness system clicks into place at once.
paras: Bengali has three yous where English has one: আপনি (apni — formal), তুমি (tumi — familiar), তুই (tui — intimate). আপনি for elders, strangers and officials; তুমি for friends, peers and younger family; তুই for childhood friends, small children and lovers. The beginner rule is simple: start at আপনি with every adult, and accept every invitation down.

Each you drags its own verb endings with it. Sit down: বসুন (boshun — formal), বসো (bosho — familiar), বস (bosh — intimate). To do: করেন, করো, কর. To go: যান, যাও, যা. The endings rhyme in threes across every verb in the language — learn the pattern once on করা and বলা, and you own it everywhere.

Moving down a level is a social ceremony. The elder says তুমি করে বলো (speak to me as তুমি) — sometimes with the words, sometimes with just a smile and a তুমি aimed at you. Mirror what you receive: if they তুমি you, তুমি them back. Asymmetry (they তুমি, you আপনি) is the natural shape of respect toward elders — don't rush to close it.

Above the yous floats one more register: সাধু ভাষা (shadhu bhasha), the old literary style of Tagore's essays, versus চলিত ভাষা (cholito bhasha), the living language of this page. তাহারা খাইতেছেন (they eat, literary) versus তারা খাচ্ছে (they eat, living). Admire the old style in books; speak the living style everywhere — nobody orders tea in সাধু ভাষা.

topics.desc: না in the wrong place, যায় for যাই, missing টা — the ten slips every learner makes, fixed. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: আমি যায় — because যায় (jay) is he/she goes, while I go is আমি যাই (ami jai). Bengali verbs change with every person, so the pronoun and the ending must match: আমি যাই, তুমি যাও, সে যায়. Drill the threes and the error dies.
faqs.q: Why is আমি যায় wrong?

faqs.a: Because Bengali verbs don't care about gender at all — সে খায় means he eats and she eats identically. Learners from Hindi or French backgrounds keep hunting for feminine endings that don't exist. There are none; celebrate.
faqs.q: Where are the feminine verb forms?

faqs.a: At the very END: আমি জানি না (I don't know), সে যাবে না (he won't go). English puts not early, Bengali puts না last — the most common word-order slip in the language, and the easiest to fix once you see it.
faqs.q: Where does না go in a sentence?

topics.note: A note on খাবার and খাওয়া. The most delicious confusion in Bengali: খাবার (khabar) is food, the thing — খাওয়া (khaoa) is eating, the act. খাবার খাওয়া (khabar khaoa — eating food) uses both at once and every learner says it backwards at least once. Food is খাবার; the eating of it is খাওয়া.
paras: Mistake one: আমি যায়. It feels right and it is wrong — যায় (jay) belongs to সে (he/she), while আমি takes যাই (jai). আমি যাই, তুমি যাও, আপনি যান: person and ending must march together. Every verb works this way, so learn verbs in threes from day one and this error never takes root.

Mistake two: hunting feminine verbs. সে খায় is he eats AND she eats — Bengali verbs never change for gender, full stop. Learners arriving from Hindi keep inventing feminine endings; stop, there are none, and this is one of the kindest simplifications in any major language. Gender lives in nouns and pronouns, never in verbs.

Mistake three: না in English position. I do not know becomes আমি জানি না — the না parks itself at the very end, after the verb. আমি না জানি sounds as broken to Bengali ears as me not knows does to yours. Rule of thumb: when in doubt, put না last and you will usually be right.

Mistake four: bare numbers on nouns. দুই বই (two books) is understood and instantly foreign — দুটো বই (duto boi) is how people speak. Things take টা/টে, people take জন: তিনটে আম (three mangoes), দুজন বন্ধু (two friends). Four mistakes, four fixes — and every one of them upgrades you from textbook speaker to real speaker the day you fix it.

topics.desc: Shadowing, self-recording and the magic sentences that turn strangers into teachers. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: ধীরে বলুন (dhire bolun — please speak slowly) and আবার বলুন (please say it again). Said with a smile, these two sentences make every Bengali speaker slow down and help — they are the learner's seatbelt and airbag.
faqs.q: What do I say when people speak too fast?

faqs.a: Yes, and it is the fastest mirror you own. Record one sentence a day — আমি বাংলা শিখছি is a fine start — and compare it weekly against the speaker buttons on this site. Ears lie to you live; recordings don't.
faqs.q: Should I record my own voice?

faqs.a: ভুল হলে শুধরে দিন (correct me if I'm wrong) said upfront turns every conversation into a free lesson. Bengalis correct kindly and love being asked — the invitation matters more than the grammar.

topics.note: A note on ঠিক করে বলেছি? Four words that buy you infinite free teaching: ঠিক করে বলেছি? (thik kore bolechhi — did I say it right?). Ask it after every brave sentence and Bengalis will fix your tones, your endings and your word order with visible joy. The learners who improve fastest are not the talented ones — they are the asking ones.
paras: Start with shadowing: play any dialogue on this site and mumble along half a beat behind the speaker, copying rhythm before words. Ten minutes of shadowing rewires your mouth faster than an hour of silent study, because Bengali lives in its lilt — the rise and fall that makes বসুন sound like an invitation instead of an order.

Then record yourself. One sentence a day — আজকের বাক্য (today's sentence) — spoken into your phone and compared against the site's speaker button. Your live ears flatter you; the recording tells the truth about your ধ, your ণ, your swallowed endings. Keep a week's recordings and the progress becomes audible, which is pure motivation fuel.

Take it outside with three brave sentences: আমি বাংলা শিখছি (I'm learning Bengali), ধীরে বলুন (please speak slowly), ভুল হলে শুধরে দিন (correct me if I'm wrong). The tea stall is the world's kindest classroom — order একটা চা দিন, answer কোথা থেকে এসেছেন? with your country, and you have had a real conversation in Bengali.

Finally, think small thoughts in Bengali. এখন চা খাব (now I'll drink tea). বাইরে বৃষ্টি (rain outside). আজ ভালো দিন (today is a good day). Nobody hears these rehearsals, but they build the reflex that matters — reaching for Bengali first instead of translating from English at the speed of panic.

faqs.a: Because real Bengali swallows endings and glues words together — আমি যাচ্ছি becomes something like ami jachchhi in a hurry. Slow the audio down, shadow it, then speed it back up: your ears learn the glued shapes by meeting them deliberately first.
faqs.q: Why do I understand lessons but not real people?

faqs.a: Songs first (slow, repeated, emotional), then serials (everyday speech, visual context), then talk shows, then news last — newsreaders speak the fastest, densest Bengali in existence. Climb the ladder in order and each rung prepares the next.
faqs.q: What should I listen to first?

faqs.a: আরেকবার বলুন (say it once more) and মানে কী? (what does it mean?). Between them you can unpack any sentence: hear it again, then interrogate the one word that sank it.

topics.note: A note on শুনতে পাচ্ছি না. Two different failures need two different sentences: শুনতে পাচ্ছি না (shunte pachchhi na — I can't hear you) is about volume, বুঝতে পারছি না (I can't understand) is about meaning. Learners mix them and get shouted at when they needed explaining to. Pick the right complaint and you get the right fix.
paras: Spoken Bengali is a different animal from written Bengali. Endings melt — করেছি sounds like korechhi with the middle chewed — words glue together, and whole syllables vanish at speed. This is not sloppy speech; it is native speech, and your first job is to stop expecting textbook sounds from human mouths.

Climb the media ladder in order. Songs: slow, repeated, and your memory holds choruses for free — গান (gaan) first. Serials and films: everyday speech with faces and plots carrying the meaning — সিনেমা (cinema) second. Talk shows third, where people interrupt each other like real life. News (খবর) last: beautiful, dense, and brutally fast.

Listen actively, not hopefully. Take one thirty-second clip and work it: first pass for gist, second pass pausing every sentence to repeat it, third pass writing what you hear, fourth pass checking against subtitles. One clip worked four ways teaches more than four hours of background radio.

Numbers and dates deserve their own drills — prices, times and phone numbers fly past at double speed in real speech. Replay market scenes and bus announcements until পঞ্চাশ টাকা and সাড়ে তিনটে land instantly. When numbers stop being noise, the whole language gets quieter and clearer.

topics.desc: Signs, menus, headlines — a script roadmap from first letters to real reading. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Two to four weeks of daily practice for the basic letters, then months of meeting conjuncts in the wild. The honest timeline: readable signs in a month, children's books in three, newspapers with a dictionary in six.
faqs.q: How long until I can read Bengali?

faqs.a: যুক্তাক্ষর (juktakkhor) — two or three consonants fused into one stack, like স্ত in স্কুল or ন্ত্র in মন্ত্র. They look terrifying and behave predictably: learn the twenty common ones and the rest surrender on sight.
faqs.q: What are those stacked letters?

faqs.a: Menus, shop signs and headlines — short, repetitive, and illustrated by reality. A week of reading signs aloud teaches more than a month of alphabet charts, because every sign you crack stays cracked.

topics.note: A note on the invisible অ. Every Bengali consonant carries a hidden অ (o) unless a vowel sign says otherwise — ক reads ko, not k. And at word ends that অ usually dies silently: ধন্যবাদ ends in a d, not da. The hidden vowel that appears and disappears is the single strangest idea in Bengali reading — master it and signs start talking.
paras: Reading Bengali starts with eleven vowels (স্বরবর্ণ) and thirty-nine consonants (ব্যঞ্জনবর্ণ), all hanging from the horizontal মাত্রা (matra) line like washing on a wire. Learn them through words you already speak — অ in অনেক, ক in কাল — and the letters arrive pre-loaded with meaning instead of as abstract squiggles.

Then come the stacks. যুক্তাক্ষর (juktakkhor) fuse consonants vertically: স + ত becomes স্ত in স্কুল and স্টেশন, ন + দ becomes ন্দ in বন্ধু. Twenty stacks cover ninety percent of daily reading — learn them as word-parts (স্কু, ষ্ট, ন্দ) rather than as letter puzzles and they stop looking scary within days.

Read the world before you read books. Shop signs (দোকান), menus (খাবারের তালিকা), bus boards, headlines — short texts where context and pictures do half the work. Read every sign aloud as you pass it; a learner who reads fifty signs a day becomes a reader in weeks, not years.

Graduate to children's books (ছোটদের বই) with big print and pictures, then comics, then headlines with a dictionary nearby. Read aloud always — Bengali spelling rewards the mouth, and hearing your own correct পড়া (reading) is the moment the script stops being a subject and becomes a skill.

faqs.a: Yes — handwriting teaches letter shapes the way typing never will, and Bengalis warm visibly to foreigners who handwrite even badly. But learn phonetic typing alongside it; you will type a hundred messages for every handwritten note.
faqs.q: Must I learn to handwrite Bengali?

faqs.a: Type Bengali sounds in Roman letters (ami, tumi, bhalo) and the keyboard converts them — Avro is the beloved classic, Google's Indic keyboard the easy start. Within days you will message in Bengali faster than you ever wrote it by hand.
faqs.q: How do I type in Bengali?

faqs.a: Three lines a night about your day: আজ ভালো দিন ছিল (today was a good day). Small, honest, daily — the diary finds your missing words for you and turns writing from homework into habit.

topics.note: A note on ই, ঈ, উ, ঊ. Bengali has short and long pairs — ই/ঈ, উ/ঊ — that sound identical in modern speech but spell differently: ইদ (Eid) versus ঈগল (eagle). Natives learn them word by word over years, so forgive yourself every mix-up and keep a small list of the ones you actually use.
paras: Writing starts at the matra line — the horizontal wire every letter hangs from. Vowels first: অ আ ই ঈ উ ঊ এ ঐ ও ঔ, each with its standalone shape and its sign-shape that clings to consonants. Write big, write slow, say each sound aloud: the hand learns what the mouth teaches it.

Consonants come in beautiful families: ক খ গ ঘ ঙ (throat), চ ছ জ ঝ ঞ (palate), ট ঠ ড ঢ ণ (roof), ত থ দ ধ ন (teeth), প ফ ব ভ ম (lips). Row by row, the mouth moves forward — chant each row and feel the sound travel. This ancient order is a pronunciation map disguised as an alphabet.

Then the stacks you write yourself: যুক্তাক্ষর like ক্ষ, জ্ঞ, স্ত. Write them as dances, not drawings — ক্ষ is ক dissolving into ষ — and practise inside real words (স্কুল, জ্ঞান, বন্ধু) rather than as isolated puzzles. Ugly stacks in real words beat pretty stacks in a chart.

Go digital with phonetic typing: type ami bhalo achhi and watch আমি ভালো আছি appear. Message friends, comment on songs, keep the diary on your phone — typed Bengali counts fully as writing, and the keyboard forgives wobbly matra lines while your handwriting catches up.

topics.desc: Verb last, না last, questions in place — the SOV skeleton of every Bengali sentence. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: I rice eat — আমি ভাত খাই. The verb goes last, always: subject, object, verb. English speakers feel the verb itch early for weeks, then one day the verb-last order clicks and English starts sounding impatient.
faqs.q: What is the basic Bengali word order?

faqs.a: Same trick, new address: আমি জানি না puts না dead last. Questions keep their question words in place too — তুমি কোথায় যাও? (you where go?) — so Bengali word order barely moves whatever the sentence does.
faqs.q: Where do না and question words go?

faqs.a: Postpositions — little location words that come AFTER the noun: টেবিলে (on the table), স্কুলে (to school), বাড়িতে (at home). English prepositions stand before; Bengali postpositions sit after. Same job, opposite side.

topics.note: A note on টা, টি and খানা. The definite article hides inside the noun: বই (a book) becomes বইটা (the book) with one small টা. টি is the polite sibling (বইটি), খানা counts flat things (দুখানা রুটি — two breads). No separate word for the — just a tail on the noun, elegant once seen.
paras: The whole skeleton is three letters: SOV. আমি (I) ভাত (rice) খাই (eat). সে (she) স্কুলে (to school) যায় (goes). The verb anchors the end of every statement, and once you stop fighting it, Bengali sentences feel calm and inevitable — everything introduced before anything happens.

Negation and questions refuse to disturb the order. আমি জানি না (I know not) parks না at the very end. তুমি কোথায় যাও? (you where go?) leaves কোথায় exactly where the answer will sit — ঢাকায় যাই (to Dhaka go). Question words are placeholders for answers, sitting in the answer's own seat.

Location words come after their nouns. টেবিলে (table-on), বাড়িতে (home-at), বাজারে (market-in): noun first, little -এ or -তে tail after. Direction works the same — ঢাকায় যাই, স্কুলে যাই. English speakers must flip every in, on and to backwards; do it deliberately for a week and it becomes reflex.

Emphasis moves to the front. ভাত আমি খাই (rice, I eat — as for rice, I eat it) topicalises ভাত without changing a single ending. Politeness softens the edges — দয়া করে বসুন (please sit) — but the skeleton never moves. SOV today, SOV tomorrow: learn it once, use it forever.

topics.desc: Your name in Bengali letters — sound mapping, tricky letters, ভালো নাম and ডাকনাম. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Map sounds, not letters: find the Bengali letter for each sound you hear. V becomes ভ, Z becomes জ, F becomes ফ, W becomes ওয়. Say your name slowly, catch each sound, stack the letters — then ask a Bengali friend to bless it.
faqs.q: How do I convert my name to Bengali?

faqs.a: Most Bengalis carry two: ভালো নাম (bhalo nam — the formal good name, on certificates) and ডাকনাম (daknam — the called name, used by everyone who loves them). Ask for both — the daknam is the friendship prize.
faqs.q: What are ভালো নাম and ডাকনাম?

faqs.a: বানান করুন (banan korun — please spell it). Then write it down immediately and read it back: নামটা দেখি? (let me see the name?). Bengalis spell patiently for learners who write carefully.

topics.note: A note on র, ড় and ঢ়. Bengali hears three r-like sounds where English hears one: র (ro, tapped), ড় (rro, flapped — the dot changes everything), ঢ় (rrho, breathy). Foreign names usually take plain র — রাহুল, রিয়া, রবার্ট. The dotted two arrive with real Bengali words; let them wait.
paras: Start with sounds, not spelling. Say your name slowly and catch each sound: R-A-H-U-L becomes রা-হু-ল — রাহুল. M-A-R-I-A becomes মা-রি-য়া — মারিয়া. English spelling lies (looking at you, silent letters); your ear tells the truth. Sounds first, letters second, always.

Some sounds need Bengali substitutes. V has no Bengali letter, so ভ steps in: ভিক্টর (Victor). Z becomes জ: জারা (Zara). F becomes ফ: ফারিয়া (Faria). W becomes ওয়: ওয়াসিম (Wasim). TH softens to থ or দ. These swaps are standard, not wrong — every Bengali reader pronounces them back correctly.

Join the letters with vowel signs, not standalone vowels. রা is র plus the া sign — one flowing shape, not two letters side by side. রি, রী, রু, রূ hang their signs above, below and around the consonant. Write your name ten times slowly and the joins become muscle memory.

Then learn the two-name tradition. ভালো নাম (bhalo nam) is the formal name on certificates — রবীন্দ্রনাথ. ডাকনাম (daknam) is the called name friends actually use — রবি. When Bengalis share their daknam with you, you have been adopted: use it, treasure it, and offer your own nickname back.

topics.desc: ফাটাফাটি, ব্যাপক, দারুণ — real slang with honest warnings about when NOT to use it. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Understand all of it, say little of it — until friends invite you in. Slang without friendship sounds like mockery; the same words with friendship sound like belonging. Let a Bengali friend be your slang licence.
faqs.q: Should beginners use slang?

faqs.a: তুই and its verbs (খাবি, যাবি, করবি) with anyone you wouldn't hug. তুই with a stranger is an insult; তুই with your best friend is love. Film heroes break this rule constantly — you are not a film hero yet.
faqs.q: What is the most dangerous slang mistake?

faqs.a: ফাটাফাটি (fatafati — awesome) is the safest superlative in Bengal: joyful, clean, and welcome from any mouth including yours. Start there; graduate to ব্যাপক when friends start laughing WITH you.

topics.note: A note on মামা and বস. On the street, মামা (mama — mother's brother) means dude and বস (bosh — boss) means mate — মামা, চা খাবি? (dude, having tea?). Lovely between friends, absurd from strangers. The rule of all slang: relationship first, words second. Earn the মামা before you spend it.
paras: Every learner's first slang word should be ফাটাফাটি (fatafati — awesome, fantastic). It is joyful, completely clean, and delights Bengalis coming from a foreign mouth — খাবারটা ফাটাফাটি (the food is awesome) has never failed anyone. Its cousins ব্যাপক (byapok — great, huge) and দারুণ (darun — wonderful) complete the safe superlative trio.

Reactions come next: ধুর (dhur — meh, nonsense) dismisses with affection, যাঃ (jah — no way!) disbelieves with delight, বাহ! (bah — wow!) applauds everything. These tiny explosions carry whole conversations — যাঃ, সত্যি? (no way, really?) — and using them right marks you as someone who listens to how Bengalis actually talk.

Now the warnings. কেটে পড় (kete poro — scram) is genuinely rude outside horseplay. ঐ (oi — hey you) summons waiters but insults peers. And everything in তুই-form — খাবি, যাবি, শোন — belongs only to close friends, children and film dialogues. Slang without the relationship is costume without the party.

Learn slang like a naturalist: collect it, label where you heard it and who said it, and deploy each word first with the friend who taught it. Slang learned from films stays in films until a living Bengali clears it for use. One cleared word a week beats fifty risky ones — and friends LOVE being your slang customs officers.

topics.desc: Animals, colours, rhymes and games — Bengali for little learners and their parents. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: ছড়া (chhora — rhymes) first: rhythm and repetition teach sounds before sense, exactly how Bengali children learn. Recite one rhyme together daily — ছড়া শোনাও (recite a rhyme) — and the language arrives disguised as play.
faqs.q: Where do kids start with Bengali?

faqs.a: Animals first (বিড়াল, কুকুর, পাখি — they move and make noises), then colours (লাল, নীল, সবুজ — the world is painted with them), then counting games. Nouns children can point at beat every abstract word.
faqs.q: Which words do children learn first?

faqs.a: Fifteen minutes of play beats an hour of lessons: naming games, colour hunts, animal sounds (বিড়াল কী বলে? — what does the cat say?). Stop while it's still fun and they'll beg to continue tomorrow.
faqs.q: How long should kids practise?

topics.note: A note on ভালো ছেলে and ভালো মেয়ে. ভালো ছেলে (good boy) and ভালো মেয়ে (good girl) are the original Bengali gold stars — say them warmly and children glow. Pair every correction with a বাহ! (wow!) for effort: Bengali parenting runs on encouragement, and little learners bloom under it.
paras: Kids learn Bengali through ছড়া (chhora — rhymes) before anything else. Rhythm teaches sounds, repetition teaches words, and actions teach meaning — clap the beats, mime the animals, march the numbers. One rhyme recited together daily (ছড়া শোনাও!) builds more Bengali than any worksheet.

Animals are the first vocabulary: বিড়াল (biral — cat), কুকুর (kukur — dog), পাখি (pakhi — bird), মাছ (machh — fish), হাতি (hati — elephant), বাঘ (bagh — tiger). Ask বিড়াল কী বলে? (what does the cat say?) and let them roar the answers — মিউ (miu), ঘেউ (gheu). Sound effects are not distractions; they are the lesson.

Colours paint the world next: লাল (lal — red), নীল (nil — blue), সবুজ (shobuj — green), হলুদ (holud — yellow), সাদা (shada — white), কালো (kalo — black). Play colour hunts — লাল কোথায়? (where is red?) — and count everything in Bengali: একটা লাল বল (one red ball). Colours plus counting is a full curriculum disguised as a game.

Keep sessions short and physical: fifteen minutes of naming games, then খেলি? (shall we play?) and ঘুমাও (sleep) at bedtime with a Bengali lullaby. Praise effort over accuracy — বাহ! for every brave word — and stop while it's still fun. The goal is a child who begs for more Bengali tomorrow, not one who survived it today.

topics.desc: Meetings, emails, deals and interviews — professional Bengali that earns respect. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: আপনি, always — with clients, seniors and strangers, in every meeting and email. Bengali workplaces run on আপনি; তুমি arrives only with genuine friendship, usually after months. Formal first is never wrong.
faqs.q: আপনি or তুমি at work?

faqs.a: Short, formal, and আপনি throughout: বিষয় (subject) first, then one clear request per email, closed with ধন্যবাদ and your name. Bengali business email is more formal than English — when in doubt, add one more দয়া করে.
faqs.q: How do I write a business email in Bengali?

faqs.a: Begin with নমস্কার and your introduction, end with a clear next step and কাল/আগামী সপ্তাহে দেখা হবে (see you tomorrow/next week). State the price plainly — দাম নিয়ে আলোচনা করি (let's discuss the price) — and confirm everything in writing.
faqs.q: How do I open and close a meeting?

topics.note: A note on মক্কেল, গ্রাহক and কাস্টমার. Three words for the people who pay: মক্কেল (mokkel — client, of a lawyer or consultant), গ্রাহক (grahok — customer, formal), কাস্টমার (customer — borrowed, everyday). Use গ্রাহক in writing, কাস্টমার in speech, মক্কেল if they signed a retainer.
paras: Work Bengali starts with introductions: আমি রাহুল, আমি গ্রামীনফোনে কাজ করি (I'm Rahul, I work at Grameenphone). আমার পদবি ব্যবস্থাপক (my title is manager). Add আপনার সঙ্গে দেখা করে ভালো লাগল (pleased to meet you) and your first meeting opens itself — formal, warm, and unmistakably professional.

Meetings run on five sentences: মিটিং কটায়? (what time is the meeting?), আজকের আলোচ্য বিষয় (today's agenda), আমি একমত (I agree), আমি ভেবে দেখব (I'll think it over), পরের সপ্তাহে আবার বসি (let's sit again next week). Master these and you can survive any meeting while your vocabulary catches up.

Money talk stays polite but plain: দাম নিয়ে আলোচনা করি (let's discuss the price), বাজেট কত? (what's the budget?), চুক্তি সই করুন (please sign the deal). Bengalis negotiate firmly and smile constantly — match both. Confirm every deal in writing the same day; spoken yeses are warm, written yeses are real.

Interviews and email close the kit. আমি এই পদের জন্য আবেদন করছি (I'm applying for this post), আমার অভিজ্ঞতা পাঁচ বছরের (I have five years' experience). In email: one request per message, আপনি throughout, ধন্যবাদ to close. Professional Bengali is just polite Bengali with the sleeves rolled up.

topics.desc: You understand everything and say nothing — the heritage learner's road back to Bengali. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Completely normal — you grew up hearing Bengali (understanding) without pressure to speak it (producing). The comprehension is buried treasure: heritage learners typically start speaking within weeks once they begin, far faster than true beginners.
faqs.q: Why do I understand but can't speak?

faqs.a: Call home weekly and hold one topic in Bengali — what you ate, the weather, your week. Grandparents are the world's most patient teachers, and ঠাকুমার সঙ্গে কথা বলা (talking with grandmother) beats any app ever made.
faqs.q: How do I practise with family?

faqs.a: দুর্গাপূজা (autumn, the great homecoming), পহেলা বৈশাখ (mid-April, the new year — শুভ নববর্ষ!), সরস্বতী পূজা (spring, goddess of learning). Festivals are language baths: go, listen, eat, repeat.
faqs.q: Which festivals should I know?

topics.note: A note on রান্নাঘরের বাংলা. Heritage Bengali often lives entirely in the kitchen — খাবার, মাছ, ভাত, ঝাল, মিষ্টি. That is not broken Bengali; it is a foundation. Food words learned at age five never leave, and every new word you add docks onto a fleet that is already floating.
paras: Heritage learners share one sentence: বুঝি কিন্তু বলতে পারি না (I understand but can't speak). You followed every family argument, laughed at every joke, and answered in English. That comprehension is not nothing — it is thousands of buried hours. Your job is not learning Bengali; it is excavating it.

Start where the language lives: home. Narrate your day to your mother in Bengali — আজ অফিসে ব্যস্ত ছিলাম (today I was busy at the office). Call your grandmother weekly: ঠাকুমা, কেমন আছেন? Family corrects with love and repeats without limit; no classroom matches a kitchen table.

Festivals are immersion you can schedule. দুর্গাপূজা brings the family home and the language with it — প্যান্ডেলে যাব (we'll go to the pandal). পহেলা বৈশাখ opens the new year with শুভ নববর্ষ (happy new year) and sweet shops. Show up, listen hard, speak badly, eat well: that is the heritage curriculum.

Fill the gaps deliberately. Kitchen Bengali needs office words, school words, street words — the registers your childhood never required. Read one children's book aloud weekly, keep the diary, and within months the buried language surfaces: first sentences, then stories, then dreams. Heritage learners don't finish last; they finish fast.

topics.desc: Weeks? Months? Years? Honest timelines for script, speech and fluency — no false promises. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: The script: two to four weeks of daily practice. First conversations: two to three months. Comfortable daily life: six to twelve months. Real fluency: one to three years. Anyone promising fluency in thirty days is selling something, not teaching something.
faqs.q: Give me the honest numbers.

faqs.a: Its close cousin Hindi needs about 1,100 class hours according to the US Foreign Service Institute — and Bengali sits in the same difficulty neighbourhood. At one hour a day, that is roughly three years; at three hours a day, about one.
faqs.q: How many hours does Bengali take?

faqs.a: Daily beats heroic: thirty focused minutes every day outperforms a five-hour Sunday. Speaking from week one, forgiving your mistakes, and living some Bengali (songs, films, one friend) multiply every hour you spend.
faqs.q: What speeds everything up?

topics.note: A note on একটু একটু. The most important phrase on this page is not a timeline but a tempo: একটু একটু (ektu ektu — little by little). Bengali rewards the steady and punishes the sprinting. Ten words a day is 3,650 words a year — more than enough to live in the language.
paras: The script surrenders first: two to four weeks of daily practice and you can sound out signs, menus and headlines. Slowly, triumphantly, aloud. This early win matters enormously — learners who can read even badly believe they can learn, and belief is half the timeline.

Speech follows in months two to six: introductions, shopping, directions, small talk about food and family — the survival kit this course teaches first. You will be slow, funny and deeply charming. Bengalis will help you mid-sentence, feed you mid-lesson, and invite you back.

Comfortable daily life arrives around month six to twelve: following conversations, handling phone calls, joking back. Real fluency — arguing, flirting, understanding films without subtitles — takes one to three years of steady contact. The honest total, via Hindi's official figure: roughly a thousand hours.

Three multipliers beat every timeline. Daily contact beats weekend heroics — প্রতিদিন (every day) is the magic word. Speaking from week one beats silent perfectionism. And one Bengali friend beats ten textbooks: হাল ছাড়বেন না (don't give up) hits different from someone waiting for your call.

topics.desc: Sister scripts, cousin words, 22 official languages — where Bengali sits in India's language family. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Cousins, through Sanskrit: both Indo-Aryan, both SOV, both with আপনি/आप formality. Shared words everywhere (পানি/पानी, বই/किताब differs though!). Hindi speakers learn Bengali fast — and Bengalis usually arrive with Hindi already loaded.
faqs.q: How close are Bengali and Hindi?

faqs.a: Twenty-two, in the Constitution's Eighth Schedule — Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Urdu, Kannada, Malayalam, Punjabi and twelve more. India has no national language; it has twenty-two official ones and hundreds of living mothers.
faqs.q: How many official languages does India have?

faqs.a: Constantly, and joyfully — Bangla-English mixing (আমি meeting-এ যাচ্ছি) mirrors Hinglish exactly. Purists grumble in both languages; everyone under forty code-switches mid-sentence. Learn the pure forms first, then join the mix.

topics.note: A note on বাংলা ভাষা. Speakers call it বাংলা (Bangla) among themselves and Bengali in English — never Bengalese, never Bengalee in modern use. বাংলা ভাষা (Bangla bhasha — the Bengali language) is the full formal name, heard in anthems, examinations and proud introductions.
paras: Bengali belongs to the Indo-Aryan family — daughter of Sanskrit, sister of Hindi, Urdu, Marathi and Gujarati, cousin to Punjabi and Nepali. Two hundred and thirty million speakers make it the world's seventh language by native speakers, and India's second after Hindi. This is not a small language you are learning; it is a civilisation.

The scripts are family portraits: Bengali অ আ ক খ and Devanagari अ आ क ख share the same ancient skeleton, the same matra wire, the same conjunct habit. Learn one script and the second comes at half price — Hindi readers decode Bengali signs within weeks, sounding them out like a familiar song in a new singer's voice.

The Dravidian south — Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam — is a different family entirely: different ancestors, different grammar deep down, though millennia of neighbours have swapped thousands of words. A Bengali in Chennai starts nearly from zero; a Bengali in Delhi starts halfway. India's language map rewards travellers who notice.

Twenty-two official languages share one constitution, and code-switching oils every border: আমি meeting-এ যাচ্ছি (I'm going to the meeting) is as natural as breathing. Respect the mix but learn the pure forms first — মাতৃভাষা (mother tongue) before mashup. Then কটা ভাষা জানেন? (how many languages do you know?) becomes your favourite bragging question.

topics.desc: মই vs আমি, বৰ vs খুব — the two closest sisters in India, compared honestly. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Partly — like Spanish and Portuguese speakers meeting slowly. Shared grammar, huge shared vocabulary, but the sounds drift: Assamese turns every স/শ/ষ into খ (kh) — অসম becomes Oxom. Give it a week of listening and the fog lifts.
faqs.q: Can Bengalis and Assamese understand each other?

faqs.a: Two letters: ৰ (Assamese ro, with its diagonal) where Bengali writes র, and ৱ (Assamese wo) with no Bengali twin. Spot a ৰ and you are reading Assamese — the single most useful letter in the northeast.
faqs.q: How do I tell the scripts apart?

faqs.a: Start with Bengali — ten times the learners, films, books and teachers — then add Assamese ears later. The grammar transfers almost whole; only the sounds and a few hundred words need relearning. Two sisters, one effort, nearly.
faqs.q: Which should I learn first?

topics.note: A note on ক্ষ, জ্ঞ and the Assamese tongue. Assamese pronounces the shared conjuncts its own way — ক্ষ sounds like khy (অসমীয়া ভাষা does things its own way, always). Don't memorise sound rules from this page; let one Assamese song retune your ears, and the sisters separate themselves.
paras: Bengali and Assamese are the closest sisters in India: neighbours along the Brahmaputra, sharers of grammar, script and most vocabulary. আমি (ami — I) in Bengali is মই (moi) in Assamese; আপনি (apni) is আপুনি (apuni); খুব (khub — very) is বৰ (bor). Same sentences, shifted sounds — learn one and the other leans in.

The scripts are twins with two tells. Assamese ৰ (ro) carries a diagonal stroke where Bengali র stands plain; Assamese ৱ (wo, as in বৰ ভাল pronounced bor bhal) has no Bengali equivalent at all. Everything else — অ আ ক খ, the matra wire, the conjunct stacks — reads identically. One diagonal letter, and you know which sister wrote it.

The great sound shift is the স-transformation: where Bengali says sh (স, শ, ষ), Assamese says kh — অসম is Oxom, not Oshom. Hear it once and every Assamese word tilts into focus; the spelling stays familiar while the mouth goes its own way. It is the single strangest and most lovable fact in either language.

Mutual understanding runs like Spanish-Portuguese: slowly, generously, with laughter. Shared words carry you (ভাল, জল, মাছ, ঘৰ/ঘর), shifted sounds test you, and goodwill translates the rest. Learn Bengali first for its ocean of books and films — then spend one week on Assamese songs, and greet the sister properly: নমস্কাৰ.

topics.desc: Ray, rhymes and the subtitle method — Bengali cinema as your most joyful teacher. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: পথের পাঁচালী (Pather Panchali, 1955) — slow, visual, human, and the most beloved doorway into Bengal ever filmed. Watch with subtitles, then without; the village speaks the clearest Bengali ever recorded.
faqs.q: Which film should I watch first?

faqs.a: Three passes, one scene: first with English subtitles for story, second with Bengali subtitles for words, third with none for ears. One ten-minute scene worked three ways teaches more than three films watched passively.
faqs.q: How do I learn from films?

faqs.a: রবীন্দ্রসঙ্গীত — Tagore's two thousand songs, the oxygen of Bengali culture — and নজরুলগীতি, the rebel poet's fire. Learn one chorus by heart (আমার সোনার বাংলা is Bangladesh's anthem) and sing it badly with joy.
faqs.q: Which songs should I learn?

topics.note: A note on টলিউড vs বলিউড. Bengali cinema is টলিউড (Tollywood — from Tollygunge, Kolkata's studio district), not Bollywood, and Bengalis notice the difference. Say টলিউড for Bengali films, বলিউড only for Hindi ones — one syllable of respect that costs nothing.
paras: Begin with the master: সত্যজিৎ রায় (Satyajit Ray), whose পথের পাঁচালী taught the world to see Bengal. His Bengali is clear, humane and slow enough for learners — অপু (Apu) speaks the village Bengali of everyone's grandparents. One Ray film with subtitles is worth a month of drills.

Use the three-pass method on every scene you love. Pass one: English subtitles, follow the story. Pass two: Bengali subtitles, catch the words — সংলাপ (dialogue) becomes study material. Pass three: no subtitles, trust your ears. Ten minutes, three passes, then move on; the film stays joyful and the Bengali sticks.

Songs are the shortcut. রবীন্দ্রসঙ্গীত (Tagore songs) play at every Bengali gathering on earth — learn আমার সোনার বাংলা and পুরানো সেই দিনের কথা phonetically first, meaning later. নজরুলগীতি brings the rebel fire. A learner who sings one chorus earns more smiles than one who conjugates ten verbs.

Talk back to the screen. Pause after a great line and repeat it — নায়ক (hero) style, full drama. ভালো লেগেছে (I liked it)? Say why, in Bengali, to the empty room. Cinema learners who speak along become conversation learners; cinema learners who only watch become subtitle readers. Be the first kind.

topics.desc: বন্ধু, ভালোবাসা, বিয়ে — friendship, love and family talk, said warmly and well. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: ভালোবাসি (bhalobashi — I love) is the deep word, for people that matter most. ভালো লাগে (bhalo lage — I like) is the everyday word, for foods, films and friends. Say ভালোবাসি rarely and mean it; say ভালো লাগে daily and smile.
faqs.q: ভালোবাসি or ভালো লাগে?

faqs.a: তোমার কথা মনে পড়ে (I remember you / I miss you) — softer and more Bengali than a direct translation of miss. For deeper missing: তোমাকে ছাড়া ভালো লাগে না (I don't feel good without you). Bengalis miss sideways, poetically.
faqs.q: How do I say I miss you?

faqs.a: প্রাণের বন্ধু (praner bondhu — friend of my soul) is the highest friendship title in the language. Bestow it rarely, earn it slowly, and never translate it back — some phrases only live in Bengali.
faqs.q: What do I call my best friend?

topics.note: A note on প্রেমিক and প্রেমিকা. প্রেমিক (premik — boyfriend) and প্রেমিকা (premika — girlfriend) are literary and slightly formal; young Bengalis often just say boyfriend/girlfriend in English. Know the Bengali words, use them in writing and elders' company, and mirror your friends everywhere else.
paras: Friendship first: বন্ধু (bondhu — friend), বন্ধুত্ব (bondhutto — friendship), প্রাণের বন্ধু (friend of my soul). Bengali friendships run deep and loud — চা খাবি? (having tea?) is a love language. Make one Bengali friend and the language stops being a subject; it becomes gossip, jokes and 2 a.m. phone calls.

Love has levels. ভালো লাগে (I like) for the everyday — তোমাকে ভালো লাগে (I like you). ভালোবাসি (I love) for the deep — তোমাকে ভালোবাসি, said rarely and meant wholly. প্রেম (prem — romance) for the poetry. Climb the ladder in order; Bengali hearts notice skipped rungs.

Marriage talk: বিয়ে (biye — wedding/marriage), বর (bor — groom), কনে (kone — bride), বিবাহিত (bibahito — married). বিয়ে কবে? (when's the wedding?) is every auntie's favourite question — learn to dodge it gracefully. Weddings are language baths: go, dance badly, speak worse, eat best.

Missing and togetherness close the heart: তোমার কথা মনে পড়ে (I miss you, poetically), একসাথে (together), সবসময় (always), সুখী (happy). সবসময় একসাথে সুখী (always happy together) — say it at weddings and watch the elders cry. Relationships are why languages exist; Bengali just says them prettier.

faqs.a: The word on the front, a PICTURE plus one example sentence on the back — never bare translation alone. মাছ → fish photo + মাছ খাই (I eat fish). Pictures dodge translation; sentences teach usage; the combo sticks twice.
faqs.q: What goes on a good card?

faqs.a: Both directions, always: Bengali→English (recognition) and English→Bengali (recall). Recognition feels easy and lies; recall feels hard and teaches. Test recall twice as often as recognition.
faqs.q: Which direction should I test?

faqs.a: Ten minutes every morning, same time, before the phone wakes up: new cards first, reviews after, mistakes re-tested tomorrow. সকালে দশ মিনিট (ten minutes in the morning) outperforms an hour of midnight cramming.

topics.note: A note on মুখস্থ. মুখস্থ (mukhostho — by heart) is the traditional Bengali way: recite until the words live in your mouth. It works beautifully for rhymes, songs and core phrases — and terribly for grammar rules. Memorise sounds with মুখস্থ; understand patterns with thinking. Both, each in its place.
paras: Build decks by topic, not by alphabet: food cards (মাছ, ভাত, ঝাল), family cards (মা, দাদা, কাকা), verb cards (যাই, খাই, করি). Topics bundle words the way life serves them — the market tests your food deck, dinner tests it again. Twenty cards per topic, no more; small decks get finished.

Make every card three-layered: Bengali word on the front; picture plus one example sentence on the back. নতুন শব্দ (new word) meets পুরনো শব্দ (old words) in every sentence — মাছ খাই reuses খাই while teaching মাছ. Cards that connect to known words stick; isolated cards slide off.

Test both directions and trust only recall. Bengali→English asks do you recognise; English→Bengali asks can you produce — ভুলে গেছি (I've forgotten) is data, not failure. Failed cards return tomorrow, then in three days, then weekly: spacing does the memorising while you sleep.

Keep the routine sacred: সকালে দশ মিনিট — ten morning minutes, new cards first, reviews after, phone still asleep. নিজেকে পরীক্ষা করুন (test yourself) before checking answers; মনে রাখুন (remember) what you missed. A year of mornings is 3,650 minutes — enough to carry five thousand words for life.

hfaqs.q: Is this Bengali course really free?
hfaqs.a: Yes — every lesson, every speaker button, every quiz. No account, no trial, no card. The course is supported by voluntary contributions on the support page.

hfaqs.q: Do I need to know Hindi first?
hfaqs.a: No. Everything is explained in plain English from zero. If you do know Hindi, the scripts are cousins and you will move faster — but nothing assumes it.
